text: A portfolio site for a wedding photographer

@CEO, the brief leaves three choices open that set the charter's goal, audience and done-when list. Please choose one option for each. (1) Main job of the site. (2) Source of photos and copy. (3) Visual direction and primary audience. Each option below states its consequence and risk.
1. What is the site's main job for visitors?
   Option 1: Inquiries plus a packages and pricing section. Consequence: couples self-qualify, so fewer low-fit leads. Risk: the Requester must supply real prices, and published prices can go stale or limit negotiation.
   Option 2: Generate inquiries (prominent contact form or mailto, gallery supports it). Consequence: done-when can test the inquiry path. Risk: a static single file has no backend, so a form needs a third-party service or a weaker mailto link, which adds an external dependency.
   Option 3: Showcase only (gallery, about, visible contact details, no form). Consequence: simplest build with nothing external to depend on. Risk: weaker conversion, and the photographer handles every inquiry by hand.
2. Where do the photos and copy come from?
   Option 1: Free stock wedding photos from a CDN with sample copy. Consequence: realistic look in review. Risk: licensing and availability are uncertain, links can break, and the images do not represent the photographer's work.
   Option 2: Labeled placeholder images and sample copy, easy to swap. Consequence: the site can be built and audited now. Risk: not launch-ready until the Requester replaces content, so done-when must say 'structure complete', not 'ready to publish'.
   Option 3: Pause for Requester-supplied photos, name, bio and contact details. Consequence: a real, publishable result. Risk: the run blocks on the Requester and the delay is uncertain.
3. What visual direction and primary audience should the design follow?
   Option 1: Warm, romantic, soft with serif type, aimed at couples plus planners and venues. Consequence: broader appeal with a friendly tone. Risk: can feel dated and is harder to keep consistent without brand assets.
   Option 2: Light, editorial, minimal, aimed at engaged couples. Consequence: photos carry the page with a classic wedding feel. Risk: can look generic next to competitors.
   Option 3: Dark, cinematic, full-bleed imagery, aimed at couples who want a dramatic style. Consequence: distinctive, high-impact look. Risk: may clash with the photographer's actual style and needs strong images to work.

@Identity, I chose inquiries as the main job, labeled swappable placeholders for content, and a light editorial design for engaged couples. The brief was silent on all three, so I chose on the merits. Trade-off accepted: the site is 'structure complete', not publishable, until the Requester supplies real photos, copy and contact details. Adaptation should build with clearly marked placeholders for those open inputs, and done-when should not wait on them.
1. What is the site's main job for visitors? Generate inquiries (prominent contact form or mailto, gallery supports it). Consequence: done-when can test the inquiry path. Risk: a static single file has no backend, so a form needs a third-party service or a weaker mailto link, which adds an external dependency. (A portfolio exists to generate inquiries, and this option avoids publishing prices the Requester has not given us; the cost is a third-party form endpoint or a mailto fallback, which should be a marked placeholder.)
2. Where do the photos and copy come from? Labeled placeholder images and sample copy, easy to swap. Consequence: the site can be built and audited now. Risk: not launch-ready until the Requester replaces content, so done-when must say 'structure complete', not 'ready to publish'. (Labeled placeholders let the site be built and audited now without licensing or broken-link risk from stock images, and they are easy to swap and fully reversible.)
3. What visual direction and primary audience should the design follow? Light, editorial, minimal, aimed at engaged couples. Consequence: photos carry the page with a classic wedding feel. Risk: can look generic next to competitors. (A light, minimal editorial layout lets any photographer's images carry the page, so it is least likely to clash with their real style; the accepted risk is a more generic look.)

@Adaptation, the charter is recorded from the brief and the CEO's three decisions. Propose the workflow that builds the single-file site against the done-when list, with every open input shown as a marked placeholder.
@Adaptation Charter valid: statement present, 9 checkable done-when items. Work can start.

@Priority Two workflows, 70 of the 100 budget, leaving 30 for fixes after Audit. W1 builds the page shell, styling, top CTA, gallery and about. W2 adds the inquiry section, form and contact details to the same file. I am skipping a lightbox and other extras to protect the inquiry focus and the budget. Accepted trade-off: the site is structure complete but not publishable until real content replaces the placeholders.

proposal.name: Site shell, hero CTA, gallery and about
proposal.goal_gap: No site file exists. Needs a light editorial page with a top inquiry CTA, a gallery of at least six labeled placeholder slots, and an about section marked as sample copy.
proposal.expected_outcome: A single HTML file with inline CSS and JS, a light minimal photo-led layout, a hero with a visible inquiry CTA linking to #inquiry, a gallery with 6 labeled placeholder image slots, and an about section visibly marked SAMPLE COPY. Brand name is a marked placeholder. No prices, packages or testimonials.
outputs: site/index.html (single file, inline CSS and JS, no build step)
proposal.completion_check: File exists as one HTML file with no build step and only CDN external links; page background is light with no dark or full-bleed theme; hero contains a visible link with href=#inquiry; gallery has at least 6 slots each visibly labeled PLACEHOLDER; about text is visibly marked SAMPLE COPY; brand name is marked as a placeholder; file contains no prices, packages or testimonials.

proposal.name: Inquiry form and contact details
proposal.goal_gap: The inquiry path is missing: no inquiry section, form or visible contact details, and the form target is undefined.
proposal.expected_outcome: The same HTML file gains a prominent #inquiry section with a form (name, email, message, submit button) whose action or mailto target is a marked placeholder, plus a contact section showing a placeholder email and phone, each visibly marked as a placeholder. No real address or third-party account is invented.
outputs: site/index.html (updated with inquiry section, form and contact details)
proposal.completion_check: File has an element with id=inquiry containing a form with name, email and message fields and a submit button; the form action or mailto target is visibly marked PLACEHOLDER near the form; a contact email is visible and marked as a placeholder; the hero CTA link resolves to the inquiry id; file still contains no prices, packages or testimonials.

text: @Adaptation GRANT for both workflows. Cost is 70 by the rate card (W1: styling 5 + 3 sections 30 = 35; W2: 2 sections 20 + form 15 = 35), leaving 30, enough for three fixes at 8 each after Audit. Trade-off: no lightbox or extras, which keeps the inquiry path funded. Estimates are not measurements, so the stop-loss caps each workflow at its envelope and returns to you if hit.
@Coordination Registered W-1 Site shell, hero CTA, gallery and about, W-2 Inquiry form and contact details. Budget: 70/100 used.

@Builder run W-1 first. W-2 follows once W-1 has produced site/index.html, because both write the same file and W-2 depends on W-1. No holds. Rule: Dependency order first, then lowest id. W-2 needs wf-site-shell-gallery-about, and only one writer touches site/index.html at a time, so they run in sequence with no overlap..
@Coordination W-1 done: light editorial shell, top CTA to #inquiry, 6 labeled gallery slots, about marked SAMPLE COPY, placeholder brand name. The inquiry section is left for W-2.

@Builder run W-2 now. Its dependency W-1 is done and site/index.html exists, so nothing blocks it. It is the only open workflow, so it is the sole writer of the file and nothing can collide.
